description: I'm Avighna Sharma. Some of my interests consist of cybersecurity, machine learning, and data analysis. I'm passionate about both attending and creating projects at hackathons, and also try my best to help provide STEM opportunities to my peers as well 🥹.
summary: Trend Detective is a web app that lets anyone drop a pin anywhere on Earth and find out whether the climate is changing there, and what it means for people. It pulls decades of NASA POWER data (MERRA-2 and CERES based) for six variables: temperature, surface heat, rainfall, sunlight, humidity and wind. It plots the time series and tests the trend with a regression t-test and the Mann-Kendall test, reporting the rate of change and whether it is statistically significant. It also ranks all six variables to show which has the clearest signal at that location, and a world scan shows the same variable rising in one place and falling in another. Plain-language explanations, a glossary, a profile of what makes each place distinctive, and an AI-assisted assessment of impacts and adaptation actions turn the statistics into something students and the public can understand and act on. It matters because climate trends are local, and most people never see the data for their own backyard.
details:
What it does. A user searches for a place or clicks the map, picks a variable and a 20-, 30- or 40-year span, and presses Investigate. The app fetches NASA POWER monthly data for that grid cell, averages it into yearly values, fits a trend line, and shows the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence band. Significance is tested two ways: a regression t-test and the Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope. We call a trend significant only when both tests agree, and the page says plainly when a trend is too weak to trust. It also shows the seasonal pattern.

Going beyond the challenge:

  • Clearest variable: it tests all six variables for the chosen spot and ranks them.
  • World scan: it maps the trend direction and significance of one variable across 16 regions.
  • Place profile: a “What makes this place special” section describes the landscape type and what scientists watch there.
  • Outlook: a projection to 2035, 2050 and 2075, labeled as a trend-continuation reference and not a forecast.
  • Human impact: each report lists variable-specific consequences for people and practical mitigation and adaptation actions.
  • AI assessment: a Groq-powered discussion of future impacts for the location. It deliberately does not invent local climate-model numbers.
  • Cost estimates: optional human-cost ranges (deaths, displacement, economic loss) built from World Bank population and GDP data and bounded by sanity caps. They are clearly labeled as estimates, with a “weak signal” warning when a trend isn’t significant.
  • Glossary: a “Words you might not know” section defines terms like anomaly, p-value and reanalysis.
  • Imagery: NASA GIBS layers sit on the map, and results can be exported as CSV.

Audience and design: We aimed at students and curious members of the public with some science background. Every statistic has a plain-English explanation, and results are shown with caveats, such as one grid cell not representing a whole region.

Tools: Python and FastAPI on the backend, which proxies NASA POWER, geocoding, and the AI and World Bank calls and keeps keys off the browser. The frontend is vanilla JavaScript with Leaflet and a CARTO basemap, with all trend statistics computed in the browser. It is deployed with Docker.

Creativity and care: We treated honesty as a feature: weak-signal warnings, bounded AI outputs, rate limits, and clear statements of what the tool cannot tell you. The impact is to make local climate evidence something anyone can check for themselves.
